title: VI. Precocity
paragraphs: "What do you think the doctor will say about him?" Kolya asked quickly. "What a repulsive mug he's got, though, hasn't he? I can't stand medicine!"
"Ilusha is dying. I think that's certain," Alyosha answered mournfully.
"They're rogues! Medicine's a fraud! I'm glad to have made your acquaintance, though, Karamazov. I've wanted to know you for a long time. I'm only sorry we're meeting under such sad circumstances."
Kolya badly wanted to say something even warmer, more heartfelt, but he felt awkward. Alyosha noticed, smiled, and pressed his hand.

"I've long since learned to respect you as someone out of the ordinary," Kolya muttered again, faltering and uncertain. "I've heard you're a mystic and that you were in the monastery. I know you're a mystic, but ... that hasn't put me off. Contact with real life will cure you of it.... It's always the way with characters like yours."
"What do you mean by mystic? Cure me of what?" Alyosha was rather taken aback.
"Oh, God and all the rest of it."
"What — don't you believe in God?"

"Oh, I've got nothing against God. Of course God's only a hypothesis, but ... I admit He's needed ... for the sake of order in the universe and all that ... and that if there were no God, He'd have to be invented," Kolya added, starting to blush. He suddenly worried Alyosha might think he was showing off his knowledge, trying to prove he was "grown up." "I haven't the slightest wish to show off my knowledge to him," Kolya thought indignantly. And all at once he felt terribly annoyed.

"I must confess I can't stand getting into discussions like this," he said, with an air of finality. "It's possible for someone who doesn't believe in God to love mankind, don't you think? Voltaire didn't believe in God, and he loved mankind?" ("There I go again," he thought to himself.)

"Voltaire did believe in God, though not very deeply, I think, and I don't believe he loved mankind very much either," Alyosha said quietly, gently, and quite naturally, as though speaking to someone his own age, or even older. Kolya was particularly struck by how tentative Alyosha seemed about his own opinion of Voltaire. He seemed to be leaving the question for him, little Kolya, to settle.
"Have you read Voltaire?" Alyosha finished.
"No, not exactly read.... But I read _Candide_, in the Russian translation ... a ridiculous, clumsy old translation ... (There I go again! Again!)"
"And did you understand it?"

"Oh, yes, all of it.... That is ... Why would you assume I wouldn't understand it? There's plenty of nastiness in it, of course.... Of course I understand that it's a philosophical novel, written to argue for an idea...." Kolya was starting to lose his footing. "I'm a Socialist, Karamazov, an incurable Socialist," he announced suddenly, apropos of nothing.
"A Socialist?" Alyosha laughed. "But when did you find the time to become one? I thought you were only thirteen?"
Kolya flinched.

"First of all, I'm not thirteen, I'm fourteen — fourteen in a fortnight," he flushed angrily, "and second, I'm completely at a loss to see what my age has to do with it. The question is what my convictions are, not what my age is, isn't it?"

"When you're older, you'll understand for yourself how age shapes convictions. And I had a feeling, too, that you weren't expressing your own ideas," Alyosha answered calmly and modestly, but Kolya broke in hotly:

"Come now, you want obedience and mysticism. You have to admit that the Christian religion, for instance, has only ever served the rich and powerful as a way to keep the lower classes in slavery. Isn't that so?"
"Ah, I know exactly where you read that, and I'm sure someone told it to you!" Alyosha cried.

"I say, what makes you think I read it somewhere? And certainly nobody told it to me. I can think for myself.... I've nothing against Christ, if you like. He was a deeply humane figure, and if He were alive today, He'd be found in the ranks of the revolutionaries, and would probably play a leading part.... There's no doubt about that."
"Oh, where, where did you get that from? What fool have you been keeping company with?" Alyosha exclaimed.
"Come, the truth will out! I'll admit I've often talked with Mr. Rakitin, of course, but ... old Byelinsky said it too, so they say."
"Byelinsky? I don't remember him writing that anywhere."
"If he didn't write it, they say he said it. I heard that from a ... but never mind."
"And have you read Byelinsky?"
"Well, no ... I haven't read all of him, but ... I read the part about Tatyana, about why she didn't go off with Onyegin."
"Didn't go off with Onyegin? Surely you don't ... understand that already?"

"Well, you seem to be taking me for little Smurov," Kolya said, with an irritated grin. "But please don't think I'm such a revolutionary. I often disagree with Mr. Rakitin. Though I bring up Tatyana, I'm not at all for the emancipation of women. I accept that women are a subject class and must obey. _Les femmes tricottent_, as Napoleon said." Kolya smiled, for some reason. "And on that question, at least, I'm entirely of one mind with that pseudo-great man. I also think that abandoning one's own country to run off to America is contemptible — worse than contemptible, foolish. Why go to America when there's so much good to be done for humanity right here? Especially now. There's a whole world of fruitful work waiting for us. That's what I told him."
"What do you mean? Told whom? Has someone already suggested you go to America?"

"I'll admit they've been after me to go, but I declined. That's strictly between us, of course, Karamazov — mind you, not a word to anyone. I only say this to you. I've no wish at all to fall into the clutches of the secret police and take lessons at the Chain Bridge.
Long will you remember The house at the Chain bridge.

Do you remember that one? It's splendid. Why are you laughing? You don't think I'm fibbing, do you?" ("What if he finds out I've only got that one issue of _The Bell_ in father's bookcase, and haven't read any more of it?" Kolya thought with a shudder.)

"Oh, no, I'm not laughing, and don't for a moment think I take you for a liar. No, indeed, I couldn't think that, because, alas, all of this is perfectly true. But tell me, have you read Pushkin — _Onyegin_, for instance? You mentioned Tatyana just now."
"No, I haven't read it yet, but I want to. I've got no prejudices, Karamazov — I want to hear both sides. Why do you ask?"
"Oh, no reason."

"Tell me, Karamazov, do you have an awful contempt for me?" Kolya suddenly rapped out, drawing himself up in front of Alyosha as though standing at drill. "Be so good as to tell me straight, without beating around the bush."
"I have contempt for you?" Alyosha looked at him, astonished. "What for? I'm only sad that a charming nature like yours should be twisted by all this crude nonsense before you've even begun living."
"Don't worry about my nature," Kolya broke in, not without some satisfaction. "But it's true I'm stupidly touchy, crudely touchy. You smiled just now, and I had the feeling you seemed to—"

"Oh, my smile meant something else entirely. I'll tell you why I smiled. Not long ago I read a piece of criticism by a German who'd lived in Russia, about our students and schoolboys today. 'Show a Russian schoolboy,' he writes, 'a map of the stars, something he knows nothing about, and he'll hand it back to you the next day with corrections.' No knowledge, and boundless conceit — that's what the German meant to say about the Russian schoolboy."

"Yes, that's exactly right," Kolya laughed suddenly, "exactly so! Bravo to the German! But he missed the good side of it, don't you think? Conceit, maybe — that comes with youth, and can be corrected if need be — but on the other hand there's an independent spirit almost from childhood, boldness of thought and conviction, and not the spirit of those sausage-makers, groveling before authority.... But the German was right all the same. Bravo, the German! Still, Germans ought to be strangled all the same. Even if they're good at science and learning, they still need strangling."
"Strangled — what for?" Alyosha smiled.

"Well, maybe I'm talking nonsense, I admit it. I'm awfully childish sometimes, and when I'm pleased about something I can't hold myself back and I'm ready to talk any amount of rubbish. But, I say, here we are chattering away about nothing, and the doctor's been in there a long time. But maybe he's examining mamma too, and that poor crippled Nina. I liked that Nina, you know. She whispered to me suddenly as I was leaving, 'Why didn't you come sooner?' And in such a voice, so reproachful! I think she's awfully sweet and pitiable."

"Yes, yes! Well, you'll be coming often, you'll see what she's like. It would do you a great deal of good to know people like that, to learn to value a great deal that you'll discover from knowing them," Alyosha said warmly. "That would do you more good than anything."
"Oh, how I regret, how I blame myself for not having come sooner!" Kolya exclaimed, with bitter feeling.
"Yes, it's a great pity. You saw for yourself how delighted the poor child was to see you. And how he ached for you to come!"

"Don't tell me! You're making it worse! But it serves me right. What kept me from coming was my conceit, my selfish vanity, and the wretched stubbornness I can never quite shake, though I've fought it my whole life. I see that now. I'm a beast in plenty of ways, Karamazov!"
"No, you have a charming nature, even if it's been twisted — and I quite understand why you've had such an influence on this generous, morbidly sensitive boy," Alyosha answered warmly.
"And you say that to me!" Kolya cried. "And would you believe it, I thought — I've thought several times since I got here — that you despised me! If only you knew how much I value your opinion!"
"But are you really so sensitive? At your age! Would you believe it — just now, while you were telling your story, I thought, watching you, that you must be very sensitive!"

"You thought that? What an eye you've got, I must say! I bet that was when I was talking about the goose. That was exactly when I imagined you had a great contempt for me for being in such a hurry to show off, and for a moment I actually hated you for it, and started babbling like a fool. Then I imagined — just now, right here — when I said that if there were no God He'd have to be invented, that I was in too much of a hurry to show off my knowledge, especially since I got that phrase out of a book. But I swear I wasn't showing off out of vanity — though I really don't know why. Because I was so pleased? Yes, I believe it was because I was so pleased ... though it's absolutely disgraceful for anyone to gush the moment they're pleased, I know that. But I'm convinced now that you don't despise me — it was all in my head. Oh, Karamazov, I'm profoundly unhappy. I sometimes imagine all sorts of things — that everyone's laughing at me, the whole world — and then I feel ready to overturn the whole order of things."
"And you make everyone around you miserable," Alyosha smiled.
"Yes, I make everyone around me miserable, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me — am I very ridiculous right now?"

"Don't think about that, don't think about it at all!" Alyosha cried. "And what does ridiculous even mean? Isn't everyone constantly being, or seeming, ridiculous? Besides, nearly all clever people nowadays are terribly afraid of looking ridiculous, and that's what makes them unhappy. All that surprises me is that you'd feel that so early — though I've noticed it for some time, and not only in you. These days even children have started suffering from it. It's almost a kind of madness. The devil has taken the shape of that vanity and slipped into this whole generation; it's simply the devil," Alyosha added, without a trace of the smile Kolya, watching him, had expected to see. "You're like everyone else," Alyosha said, in conclusion, "that is, like a great many others. Only you mustn't be like everyone else — that's all."
"Even if everyone is like that?"

"Yes, even if everyone is like that. Be the one who isn't. You really aren't like everyone else — here you are, not ashamed to admit to something bad, even ridiculous. And who admits to that much these days? No one. People have even stopped feeling the urge to examine themselves. Don't be like everyone else, even if you're the only one who isn't."

"Wonderful! I wasn't wrong about you. You know how to give comfort. Oh, how I've longed to know you, Karamazov! I've been eager for this meeting a long time. Can you really have thought about me too? You said just now you'd thought of me too?"
"Yes, I'd heard of you and had thought about you too ... and if it's partly vanity that makes you ask, it doesn't matter."
"Do you know, Karamazov, this conversation of ours has been rather like a declaration of love," Kolya said, in a bashful, melting voice. "That's not ridiculous, is it?"
"Not at all ridiculous, and even if it were, it wouldn't matter, because it's been a good thing." Alyosha smiled brightly.
"But you know, Karamazov, you have to admit you're a little ashamed yourself right now.... I can see it in your eyes." Kolya smiled with a sly sort of happiness.
"Why ashamed?"
"Well, why are you blushing?"
"It's you who made me blush," Alyosha laughed, and he really did blush. "Oh, well, a little, heaven knows why, I don't know..." he muttered, nearly embarrassed.
"Oh, how I love and admire you at this moment, precisely because you're a little ashamed! Because you're just like me," Kolya cried, in real ecstasy. His cheeks glowed, his eyes shone.
"You know, Kolya, you're going to be very unhappy in your life," something made Alyosha say suddenly.
"I know, I know. How do you know it all in advance!" Kolya agreed at once.
"But you'll bless life on the whole, all the same."

"Exactly so, hurrah! You're a prophet. Oh, we'll get on well together, Karamazov! Do you know what delights me most? That you treat me completely as an equal. But we're not equals — no, we're not, you're better! But we'll get on. You know, all this last month I've been telling myself, 'Either we'll be friends at once, forever, or we'll part as enemies to the grave!'"
"And saying that, of course, you already loved me," Alyosha laughed cheerfully.
"I did. I loved you terribly. I've been loving you and dreaming about you. And how do you know it all in advance? Ah, here's the doctor. Goodness! What will he tell us? Look at his face!"
